# Semester 2

## Week 1

### For Discussion
- No matter how many times I try to generate population and ensure introduction of covariance, nothing "feels right"
- Given we're dealing with categorical variables here, especially ones that should largely be independent, I don't see the actual point of this still either. Particularly given all we are trying to test is whether the output is as good as the input anyway--rendering the actual "quality" of the input irrelevant.
- The only way to actually covary is to have a latent score in the background, but this isn't entirely intuitive for these variables and, once again, seems to be at least partially besides the point here. What does it mean to be in the "top percentile of gender"?
- Even if I do bin percentiles for categories, by assuming relationships between them, it makes weird and unrealistic messes anyway. E.g. If I split the latent scores into male (lowest percentile), female (middle percentile), non-binary (top percentile)--I would/could make the assumption that less older people would identify as non-binary, and so inversely correlate it with the latent scores of age. But this would then also mean older people are more likely to be men and middle-age people are more likely to be women.

- Particularly given I'm working with multivariate normals, I could understand trying to do this ordinally, but with nominal demographic variables specifically, this feels a bit sanity-breaking, unless I am missing something super obvious.
- Multimodal copulas could be an option but seem like excessive work, given the focus is assessing whether output matches input and not whether the input was "realistic".

- Can I, instead, generate as purely independent and random (as I did previously), then measure level of association (covariance) with Cramer V, report this, and measure and compare against Cramer V in the following samples/panels?
    - Though this may not even be possible either, since our intersectional slices will be pretty small by the final panel level
